results.location: 1.1 Our results
results.content: Theorem 1.1 (Informal restatement of Corollary C.5): "Fix any convex set 𝒫 (with no restrictions on symmetry or other geometric properties) and any norm ‖·‖ (including non-standard norms). Assume there exists a function R : 𝒫 → ℝ that is 1-strongly-convex with respect to ‖·‖ and has range (max_{x ∈ 𝒫} R(x) − min_{x ∈ 𝒫} R(x)) at most ρ. Then TreeCal guarantees that the calibration error of its predictions is bounded by Cal_T^{‖·‖} ≤ εT for T ≥ (diam_{‖·‖}(𝒫)/ε)^{O(ρ/ε²)} for all possible choices of 𝒫 and ‖·‖."
results.route_rationale: Informal restatement of Corollary C.5; algorithmic guarantee, not a crisp formal algebraic claim.

results.location: 1.1 Our results
results.content: Corollary 1.2 (Informal restatement of Corollary C.6): "Let 𝒫 ⊆ ℝ^d be a centrally symmetric convex set, and let 𝓛 = {y ∈ ℝ^d | ‖y‖_* ≤ 1} for some norm ‖·‖. Then if there exists an algorithm for online linear optimization with action set 𝒫 and loss set 𝓛 that incurs regret at most O(√(ρT)), TreeCal guarantees that the calibration error of its predictions is bounded by Cal_T^{‖·‖} ≤ εT for T ≥ (diam_{‖·‖}(𝒫)/ε)^{O(ρ/ε²)}."
results.route_rationale: Informal restatement of Corollary C.6.

results.location: 1.1 Our results
results.content: Theorem 1.3 (Informal restatement of Theorem 3.1): "Fix a convex set ℘ and a norm ‖·‖. Assume there exists a function R : ℘ → ℝ that is 1-strongly-convex with respect to ‖·‖ and has range (max_{x∈℘} R(x) − min_{x∈℘} R(x)) at most ρ. Then TreeCal guarantees that the calibration error of its predictions is bounded by Cal_T^{‖·‖²} ≤ ε T for T ≥ (diam_{‖·‖}(℘)/√ε)^{O(ρ/ε)}."
results.route_rationale: Informal restatement of Theorem 3.1.

results.location: 1.1 Our results
results.content: Theorem 1.4 (Informal restatement of Theorem 4.3): "There is a sufficiently small constant c > 0 so that the following holds. Fix any ε > 0, d ∈ ℕ. Then for any T ≤ exp(c · min{d^{1/14}, ε^{−1/6}}), there is an oblivious adversary producing a sequence of outcomes so that any learning algorithm must incur ℓ1-calibration error Cal_T^{‖·‖₁} ≥ ε · T."
results.route_rationale: Informal restatement of Theorem 4.3.

results.location: 1 Introduction
results.content: Definition of calibration error in the introduction: "Cal_T^{‖·‖} = Σ_{t=1}^T ‖p_t − ν_{p_t}‖, where ν_{p_t} is the average of the outcomes y_t on rounds where the learner predicted p_t." (The formal definition in Section 2.1 reads Cal_T^D(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) := Σ_{p ∈ 𝒫} ((1/T) Σ_{t=1}^T x_t(p)) · D(ν_p, p), which differs from this display by a factor of T.)
results.route_rationale: Central definition; check consistency between the intro display and the formal definition.

results.location: 2.3 From swap regret to calibration
results.content: "Given a convex function R : 𝒫 → ℝ, the Bregman divergence associated to R, D_R : 𝒫 × 𝒫 → ℝ_{≥0}, is defined as D_R(y ‖ p) := R(p) − R(y) − ⟨∇R(y), p − y⟩. Geometrically, this divergence is defined by taking the hyperplane tangent to R at p and computing the difference in height between R and the hyperplane at y."
results.route_rationale: Definition that is inconsistent with its own geometric description and with every subsequent use (proof of Lemma 2.1, strong-convexity equivalence, proofs of Lemmas 2.4/3.2).

results.location: 2.4 Rates and regularization
results.content: "We say that a convex function R : 𝒫 → ℝ is α-strongly convex with respect to a given norm ‖·‖ if for any points y, p ∈ 𝒫 it is the case that R(y) ≤ R(p) + ⟨∇R(p), y − p⟩ + α‖y − p‖². Equivalently, the Bregman divergence must satisfy D_R(y ‖ p) ≥ α‖y − p‖²."
results.route_rationale: Definition; the displayed inequality direction is inconsistent with the claimed equivalence and with standard strong convexity.

results.location: 2.4 Rates and regularization
results.content: "Each algorithm in this class is specified by a convex 'regularizer' function R : 𝒫 → ℝ, and at round t selects the action p_t = argmin_{p∈𝒫} Σ_{s=1}^{t−1} ⟨p, ℓ_s⟩ + R(p)."
results.route_rationale: Definition of FTRL; no property asserted that could be false.

results.location: 2.3 From swap regret to calibration
results.content: Lemma 2.1: "For any 𝐲 ∈ Δ(𝒫) and convex function R : 𝒫 → ℝ, let ȳ = 𝔼_{y∼𝐲}[y], and \overline{R(y)} = 𝔼_{y∼𝐲}[R(y)]. For all p ∈ 𝒫, 𝔼_{y∼𝐲}[D_R(y ‖ p)] = D_R(ȳ ‖ p) + \overline{R(y)} − R(ȳ). In particular, ℓ(p) = 𝔼_{y∼𝐲}[D_R(y ‖ p)] is minimized at p = ȳ at a value of \overline{R(y)} − R(ȳ)."
results.route_rationale: Clean algebraic identity; suspected inconsistency with the printed Bregman definition makes it a refutation candidate.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised Lemma 2.1 exactly as printed, with the printed Bregman divergence D_R(y‖p) := R(p) − R(y) − ⟨∇R(y), p − y⟩ (gradient at the first argument), instantiated to the two-point distribution y = 0 w.p. 1/2, y = 1 w.p. 1/2 (ȳ = 1/2, E[R(y)] = (R 0 + R 1)/2). Lean proved the negation (theorem lemma21_refuted, file Paper/Verified/paper__LEMMA__0.lean): at R(x) = x^4, grad(x) = 4·x^3, p = 0, the LHS is 3/2 while the RHS is 5/8, so the printed identity is false. Under the corrected convention D_R(y‖p) = R(y) − R(p) − ⟨∇R(p), y − p⟩ (gradient at the second argument — the convention every proof in the paper actually uses), the identity holds for ANY R and grad (theorem lemma21_correct_2point compiles clean). Hence the printed Bregman definition is the typo; the lemma is true under the intended convention.

lean.formal_statement: theorem lemma21_refuted : ¬ (∀ (R : ℝ → ℝ) (grad : ℝ → ℝ) (p : ℝ), (1/2) * bregmanPrinted R grad 0 p + (1/2) * bregmanPrinted R grad 1 p = bregmanPrinted R grad (1/2) p + ((R 0 + R 1)/2) - R (1/2))
lean.compiler_feedback: Clean compile. `lake env lean Paper/TMP.lean` exit 0; no severity-1 diagnostics; axioms are the standard Mathlib set.

results.location: 2.3 From swap regret to calibration
results.content: Lemma 2.2: "Fix any convex function R : 𝒫 → ℝ. For any sequence of distributions x_1, x_2, …, x_T ∈ Δ(𝒫) and outcomes y_1, y_2, …, y_T ∈ 𝒫, define the sequence of loss functions ℓ_1, ℓ_2, …, ℓ_T via ℓ_t(p) = D_R(y_t ‖ p). Then, FullSwapReg_T(x_{1:T}, ℓ_{1:T}) = Cal_T^{D_R}(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T})."
results.route_rationale: FullSwapReg = Cal identity; involves sup over arbitrary swap functions π : 𝒫 → 𝒫, not a crisply formalisable finite claim.

results.location: B Proofs of preliminary results
results.content: Proof of Lemma 2.1: "𝔼_{y∼𝐲}[D_R(y‖p)] = 𝔼_{y∼𝐲}[R(y) − R(p) − ⟨∇R(p), y − p⟩] = \overline{R}(ȳ) − R(p) − ⟨∇R(p), ȳ − p⟩ = D_R(ȳ‖p) + \overline{R}(ȳ) − R(ȳ)."
results.route_rationale: Proof that contradicts the printed Bregman definition (uses the gradient-at-p convention).

results.location: B Proofs of preliminary results
results.content: Proof of Lemma 2.2 (key steps): "FullSwapReg_T(x_{1:T}, ℓ_{1:T}) = sup_{π:𝒫→𝒫} Σ_t Σ_{p∈𝒫} x_t(p)·(ℓ_t(p) − ℓ_t(π(p))) = Σ_{p∈𝒫} max_{p*∈𝒫} Σ_t x_t(p)·(ℓ_t(p) − ℓ_t(p*)) = Σ_{p∈𝒫} max_{p*∈𝒫} Σ_t x_t(p)·(D_R(y_t|p) − D_R(y_t|p*)) = Σ_{p∈𝒫} Σ_t x_t(p)·D_R(ν_p|p) = Cal_T^{D_R}(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T})."
results.route_rationale: sup-π exchange and weighted Bregman-mean argument.

results.location: 2.4 Rates and regularization
results.content: Theorem 2.3: "Let 𝒫 and 𝓛 be centrally symmetric convex sets. Then, if the function R : 𝒫 → ℝ is 1-strongly convex with respect to the norm ‖·‖_{𝓛*} and has range ρ (i.e., max_{p∈𝒫} R(p) − min_{p∈𝒫} R(p) = ρ), then Rate_OLO(𝒫, 𝓛) ≤ ρ. Conversely, there exists a function R : 𝒫 → ℝ that is 1-strongly convex with respect to ‖·‖_{𝓛*} and has range O(Rate_OLO(𝒫, 𝓛))."
results.route_rationale: Quoted FTRL/GSJ24 result; no derivation to check in the excerpt.

results.location: 2.4 Rates and regularization
results.content: Lemma 2.4: "If the action set 𝒫 is centrally symmetric and 𝓛 = {y ∈ ℝ^d | ‖y‖_* ≤ 1} (i.e., the unit ball in the dual norm to ‖·‖), then Rate_OLO(𝒫, 𝓛) = Θ(Rate(𝒫, ‖·‖))."
results.route_rationale: Asymptotic equivalence; the construction proof is in Appendix B (checked separately).

results.location: B Proofs of preliminary results
results.content: Proof of Lemma 2.4 (construction R′(p) = 4R(p/2)): "If R is 1-strongly convex, then R(p/2) is 1/4-strongly convex, and so R′ is also 1-strongly convex. … for any z_1, z_2 ∈ 𝒫, ⟨∇R(z_1/2), z_2⟩ ≤ 2ρ. … max_{y,p∈𝒫} D_{R′}(y|p) = R′(y) − R′(p) − ⟨∇R′(p), y − p⟩ = 4R(y/2) − 4R(p/2) − 2⟨∇R(p/2), y − p⟩ ≤ 4|R(y/2) − R(p/2)| + 2(⟨∇R(p/2), y⟩ − ⟨∇R(p/2), p⟩) ≤ 4ρ + 4ρ = 8ρ."
results.route_rationale: Convex-analysis inequality chain; the displayed arithmetic is checkable by hand.

results.location: 3.2 Main result
results.content: Theorem 3.1 (Main theorem): "Let P ⊂ R^d be a bounded convex set and ‖·‖ be an arbitrary norm. Then, TreeCal (Algorithm 1) guarantees that for an arbitrary sequence of outcomes y_1, …, y_T ∈ P, the ‖·‖² calibration error of its predictions x_1, …, x_T ∈ Δ(P) is bounded as follows: Cal_T^{‖·‖²}(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) ≤ ε T for T ≥ (diam(P)/√ε)^{O(Rate(P, ‖·‖)/ε)}."
results.route_rationale: Main algorithmic guarantee; statement-level consistency check.

results.location: 3.3 Outline of the proof of Theorem 3.1
results.content: Equation (5): "Cal_T^{‖·‖²}(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) ≤ Cal_T^{D_R}(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) = FullSwapReg_R(x_{1:T}, ℓ_{1:T}), where ℓ_t : P → R is the loss function given by ℓ_t(p) := D_R(y_t ‖ p); the inequality uses strong convexity of R, and the subsequent equality uses Lemma 2.2."
results.route_rationale: Reduction inequality; strong-convexity and Lemma 2.2 step.

results.location: 3.3 Outline of the proof of Theorem 3.1
results.content: Lemma 3.2: "Let P ⊂ R^d be a bounded convex set and let R : P → R be a convex function. For a sequence of loss functions ℓ_1, …, ℓ_H : P → R, define FTL_h(ℓ_{1:H}) = argmin_{p∈P} Σ_{s=1}^{h−1} ℓ_s(p). For all sequences of outcomes y_{1:T} ∈ P^T, the action distributions x_t produced by TreeCal on y_{1:T} equal those produced by TreeSwap.FTL on loss functions ℓ_t(p) = D_R(y_t ‖ p) for all t."
results.route_rationale: TreeCal = TreeSwap.FTL equivalence; proper-scoring-rule argument.

results.location: C.2 Proof of the main theorem
results.content: Proof of Theorem 3.1 (condensed): "Lemma 3.2 gives the actions are identical to TreeSwap.FTL. Let \tilde p_{k,h}^{(l)} = BTL_{h+1}(ℓ_{k,0}^{(l)},…,ℓ_{k,h}^{(l)}) be the BTL actions. Claim C.3: Cal_T^{‖·‖²}(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) − 2·Cal_T^{‖·‖²}(x̃_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) ≥ (2·diam(𝒫)²/H²)·T. … ExtReg_H(BTL_H) ≤ 0, so by Theorem C.1, FullSwapReg_T(x̃_{1:T}, ℓ_{1:T}) ≤ T·(3ρ)/L. … Cal_T^{‖·‖²}(x) ≤ 2·Cal_T^{‖·‖²}(x̃) + (2·diam(𝒫)²/H²)·T ≤ 2·Cal_T^{D_R}(x̃) + (2·diam(𝒫)²/H²)·T = 2·FullSwapReg_T(x̃, D_R(y_{1:T}[·])) + (2·diam(𝒫)²/H²)·T ≤ (6ρ·T)/L + (2·diam(𝒫)²·T)/H². Given ε > 0, choosing L = 12ρ/ε and H = diam(𝒫)/√ε gives Cal_T^{‖·‖²}(x) ≤ ε·T as long as T ≥ H^L = (diam(𝒫)/√ε)^{12ρ/ε}."
results.route_rationale: Main-theorem proof chain; verify Claim C.3 use, the parameter arithmetic, and the final bound.

results.location: 4 Lower bound
results.content: Theorem 4.1 (Theorem 4.1 of [DFG^+24]): "There is a sufficiently small constant c_{4.1} > 0 … Fix any ε > 0. For any d ∈ ℕ, there is a subset 𝒳 ⊂ [−1, 1]^d so that for any T ≤ exp(c_{4.1} min{d^{1/14}, ε^{−1/6}}) there is an oblivious adversary producing v_1, …, v_T with ‖v_t‖_1 ≤ 1 and ‖v_t‖_∞ ≤ max{d^{−13/14}, ε^{13/6}}, such that for linear losses ℓ(x, v) = ⟨v, x⟩, any learning algorithm producing x_1, …, x_T ∈ Δ(𝒳) satisfies FullSwapReg_T(x_{1:T}, ℓ(·, v_{1:T})) ≥ ε·T."
results.route_rationale: Quoted external lower bound; internal-consistency check only.

results.location: 4 Lower bound
results.content: Theorem 4.3: "There is a sufficiently small constant c > 0 so that the following holds. Write D(p, p′) = ‖p − p′‖_1, and fix any ε > 0, d ∈ ℕ. Then for any T ≤ exp(c · min{d^{1/7}, ε^{−1/6}}), there is an oblivious adversary producing a sequence y_1, …, y_T ∈ Δ^d so that for any learning algorithm producing x_1, …, x_T ∈ Δ(Δ^d), Cal_T^D(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) ≥ ε · T."
results.route_rationale: Lower-bound statement; the d-exponent here (1/7) conflicts with the abstract, intro (1/14), and the proof.

results.location: 4 Lower bound
results.content: Lemma 4.2: "Fix a set 𝒫 ⊂ ℝ^d, a norm ‖·‖, and write D(p, p′) := ‖p − p′‖. Suppose that, for some ε > 0, T ∈ ℕ, there is an algorithm which chooses x_1, …, x_T ∈ Δ(𝒫) and which ensures that for every oblivious adversary choosing y_1, …, y_T ∈ 𝒫, we have Cal^D(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) ≤ ε·T. Then for every set 𝒫′ ⊂ ℝ^d, there is an algorithm which chooses x′_1, …, x′_T ∈ Δ(𝒫′) and which ensures that for every oblivious adversary choosing y_1, …, y_T ∈ 𝒫, we have FullSwapReg_T(x′_{1:T}, ℓ(·, y_{1:T})) ≤ ε·T·diam_{‖·‖_*}(𝒫′)."
results.route_rationale: Calibration-to-swap-regret reduction; dual-norm diameter factor.

results.location: D.1 Lower bound on ℓ1 calibration
results.content: Proof of Lemma 4.2 (key lines): "FullSwapReg_T(x′_{1:T}, ℓ(·, y_{1:T})) = sup_{π:𝒫′→𝒫′} Σ_{p∈𝒫} Σ_{t∈[T]} x_t(p)·⟨y_t, BR(p) − π(BR(p))⟩ = sup_π Σ_{p∈𝒫} (Σ_t x_t(p))·⟨ν_p, BR(p) − π(BR(p))⟩ ≤ sup_π Σ_{p∈𝒫} (Σ_t x_t(p))·(‖ν_p − p‖·‖BR(p) − π(BR(p))‖_*) ≤ diam_{‖·‖_*}(𝒫′)·Cal^D_T(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T})."
results.route_rationale: BR best-response + Hölder + dual-norm diameter bound.

results.location: D.1 Lower bound on ℓ1 calibration
results.content: Proof of Theorem 4.3: "Suppose to the contrary … By Lemma D.1, for d′ = ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ there is an algorithm Alg′ for calibration on B^{d′}_1 … We now apply Lemma 4.2 for 𝒫 = B^{d′}_1, the norm ‖·‖_1, and 𝒫′ := [−1,1]^{d′}. Note that diam_{‖·‖_∞}(𝒫′) = 1. Then Lemma 4.2 ensures … FullSwapReg_T(x″_{1:T}, ℓ(·, y″_{1:T})) ≤ ε·T. But if T ≤ exp(c_{4.1}·min{(d′)^{1/14}, ε^{−1/6}}), we have a contradiction to Theorem 4.1."
results.route_rationale: Contradiction argument; the claimed diameter value is checkable.

results.location: C.1 Labeled calibration and swap regret
results.content: Theorem C.1 (TreeSwap; Theorem 3.1 of [DDFG24]): "Suppose that H, L ∈ ℕ satisfy H ≥ 2 and H^{L−1} ≤ T ≤ H^L. For bounded convex action set 𝒫 ⊂ ℝ^d and loss function set 𝓛 ⊂ {ℓ : 𝒫 → [0, b]}, let Alg_H : 𝓛^H → 𝒫^H be any algorithm. Then, the labeled TreeSwap algorithm parametrized by T, H, L, 𝒫, 𝓛, Alg_H outputs labeled distributions x_1, …, x_T ∈ Δ(𝒫̄) satisfying: for any sequence ℓ_1, …, ℓ_T ∈ 𝓛, FullSwapReg_T(x_{1:T}, ℓ_{1:T}) ≤ T·(ExtReg_H(Alg_H)/H + b/L)."
results.route_rationale: Quoted external TreeSwap guarantee.

results.location: C.1 Labeled calibration and swap regret
results.content: Equation (6): "Cal_T^D(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) = Σ_{l=1}^L (H^{L−l}/L) Σ_{k ∈ [H]^l} D(ȳ_k^{(l)}, p_k^{(l)}), as each level l action is selected with 1/L mass for H^{L−l} rounds."
results.route_rationale: Labeled-calibration level sum; verify the H^{L−l}/L mass factors.

results.location: C.2 Proof of the main theorem
results.route_rationale: Notation definitions; self-consistency check.

results.location: C.2 Proof of the main theorem
results.content: Lemma C.2: "Fix distributions q_0, …, q_h ∈ Δ(𝒫), and define ℓ_i(p) := E_{y∼q_i}[D_R(y‖p)]. Then for each h > 0, FTL_h(ℓ_0, …, ℓ_{h−1}) = (1/h) Σ_{i=0}^{h−1} E_{y∼q_i}[y]."
results.route_rationale: FTL = average; proper-scoring-rule consequence of Lemma 2.1.

results.location: C.2 Proof of the main theorem
results.route_rationale: Expansion used in Claim C.3; check mass factors.

results.location: C.2 Proof of the main theorem
results.content: Claim C.3 and its proof: Claim: "Cal_T^{‖·‖²}(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) − 2·Cal_T^{‖·‖²}(x̃_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) ≥ (2·diam(𝒫)²/H²)·T. (9)" Proof: "Cal − 2Cal(x̃) = Σ_{l,h} (H^{L−l}/L)(‖ν_{h} − p‖² − 2‖ν_{h} − \tilde p‖²) (11) ≤ 2 Σ_{l,h} (H^{L−l}/L)‖p − \tilde p‖² ≤ (2/L) Σ_l Σ_{h_{1:l−1}} diam(𝒫)² · H^{L−l} ≤ (2/L) Σ_l diam(𝒫)² · H^{L−1} = (2T·diam(𝒫)²)/H."
results.route_rationale: Claim statement vs its own proof: direction and H-exponent both disagree.

results.location: C.2 Proof of the main theorem
results.content: Lemma C.4: "Fix any convex set 𝒫 ⊂ ℝ^d and a convex function R : 𝒫 → ℝ. Fix a sequence y_1,…,y_H ∈ 𝒫, and set p_h = (1/(h−1)) Σ_{i=1}^{h−1} y_i for all h ∈ [H], h>1, and \tilde p_h = (1/h) Σ_{i=1}^h y_i for all h ∈ [H], as well as p_1 ∈ 𝒫 arbitrarily. Then Σ_{h=1}^H ‖p_h − \tilde p_h‖² ≤ 2·diam(𝒫)²."
results.route_rationale: Clean inequality on cumulative averages; formally verifiable in a normed space.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised Lemma C.4 in a real normed vector space E: for a convex set P with pairwise distances ≤ D, points y_0..y_{H−1} ∈ P, p_1 ∈ P, with a_h = (1/h)Σ_{i<h} y_i, proved theorem lemma_C4 : ‖p1 − a_1‖² + Σ_{k=1}^{H−1} ‖a_k − a_{k+1}‖² ≤ 2·D² (file Paper/Verified/paper__LEMMA__6.lean). Proof: (i) gap identity a_{h+1} − a_h = (y_h − a_h)/(h+1); (ii) ‖a_{h+1} − a_h‖ ≤ D/(h+1) using convexity of P (a_h ∈ P) and the diameter bound; (iii) Σ_{k} 1/(k+2)² ≤ 1 by telescoping 1/((k+1)(k+2)) = 1/(k+1) − 1/(k+2); (iv) ‖p_1 − a_1‖ ≤ D. The lemma is true. (The paper's own printed proof, in contrast, only bounds one term and is incomplete — see paper::PROOF::5.)

lean.formal_statement: theorem lemma_C4 {P : Set E} (hP : Convex ℝ P) {D : ℝ} (hD : 0 ≤ D) (hPdiam : ∀ ⦃x⦄, x ∈ P → ∀ ⦃y⦄, y ∈ P → ‖x - y‖ ≤ D) {H : ℕ} (hH : 1 ≤ H) (y : ℕ → E) (hy : ∀ i < H, y i ∈ P) (p1 : E) (hp1 : p1 ∈ P) : ‖p1 - avg y 1‖^2 + Finset.sum (Finset.range (H - 1)) (fun k => ‖avg y (k + 1) - avg y (k + 2)‖^2) ≤ 2 * D^2

results.location: C.2 Proof of the main theorem
results.content: Proof of Lemma C.4: "Proof. Note that \tilde p_h − p_h = y_h/h − (1/(h(h−1))) Σ_{i=1}^{h−1} y_i, which implies that ‖\tilde p_h − p_h‖² ≤ (π²/6)·diam(𝒫)² < 2·diam(𝒫)². □"
results.route_rationale: The printed proof bounds only one term; the lemma's conclusion is a sum over h = 1..H.

results.location: C.2 Proof of the main theorem
results.content: Proof of Corollary C.5 (Jensen step): "Using Σ_{p∈𝒫} Σ_{t=1}^T x_t(p) = T and Jensen: (1/T)·Cal_T^{‖·‖}(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) = (1/T) Σ_p (Σ_t x_t(p))·‖ν_p − p‖ ≤ √((1/T) Σ_p (Σ_t x_t(p))·‖ν_p − p‖²) = √((1/T)·Cal_T^{‖·‖²}(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T})) ≤ ε for T ≥ (diam(𝒫)/ε)^{O(Rate(𝒫,‖·‖)/ε²)} by Theorem 3.1."
results.route_rationale: Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz / Jensen step and the ε→ε² exponent rescaling.

results.location: D.1 Lower bound on ℓ1 calibration
results.content: Lemma D.1: "Fix d ∈ ℕ, and write D(x, y) := ‖x − y‖_1. Suppose that there is an algorithm Alg for calibration over the domain P = Δ^{2d+1} which produces x_{1:T} given y_{1:T} achieving calibration error Cal^D_T(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) ≤ R(T). Then there is an algorithm Alg′ for calibration over the domain B^d_1 which produces x′_{1:T} given y′_{1:T} achieving Cal^D_T(x′_{1:T}, y′_{1:T}) ≤ R(T)."
results.route_rationale: Reduction between simplex and ℓ1-ball calibration.

results.location: D.1 Lower bound on ℓ1 calibration
results.content: The φ/ψ construction (Lemma D.1): "φ(y)_i = { [y_j]_+ : i = 2j − 1, j ∈ [d]; [y_j]_- : i = 2j, j ∈ [d]; 1 − ‖y‖_1 : i = 2d + 1 }, ψ(z)_i = z_{2i−1} − z_{2i}, i ∈ [d], so that ψ ∘ φ(y) = y for all y ∈ B^d_1."
results.route_rationale: Componentwise identity [t]_+ − [t]_- = t and simplex membership of φ(y); formally verifiable.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised the mathematical core of the φ/ψ construction (file Paper/Verified/paper__EQUATION__7.lean): (i) psi_phi_id — for every coordinate, [y_j]_+ − [y_j]_- = y_j, i.e. ψ∘φ = id componentwise (posPart_sub_negPart); (ii) phi_components_sum_one — the 2d+1 components of φ(y) (the [y_j]_+, [y_j]_- and the slack 1 − ‖y‖_1) sum to 1, using [t]_+ + [t]_- = |t| and Σ_j |y_j| = ‖y‖_1; (iii) phi_components_nonneg — all components are ≥ 0 when ‖y‖_1 ≤ 1. Together these establish φ(y) ∈ Δ^{2d+1} and ψ∘φ(y) = y on B^d_1, as claimed in Lemma D.1. The Fin(2d+1) repacking of the components is definitional bookkeeping.

lean.formal_statement: theorem psi_phi_id {d : ℕ} (y : Fin d → ℝ) : (fun j : Fin d => posP (y j) - negP (y j)) = y; theorem phi_components_sum_one {d : ℕ} (y : Fin d → ℝ) : (∑ j, posP (y j)) + (∑ j, negP (y j)) + (1 - ∑ j, |y j|) = 1; theorem phi_components_nonneg {d : ℕ} (y : Fin d → ℝ) (h : (∑ j, |y j|) ≤ 1) : (∀ j, 0 ≤ posP (y j)) ∧ (∀ j, 0 ≤ negP (y j)) ∧ 0 ≤ 1 - ∑ j, |y j|

results.location: D.1 Lower bound on ℓ1 calibration
results.content: Proof of Lemma D.1 (key lines): "ψ(φ(y))_i = [y_i]_+ − [y_i]_- = y_i … φ(y) ∈ Δ^{2d+1} since components ≥ 0 (‖y‖_1 ≤ 1) and Σ_i φ(y)_i = Σ_j ([y_j]_+ + [y_j]_-) + 1 − ‖y‖_1 = Σ_j |y_j| + 1 − ‖y‖_1 = 1 … ν′_{p′} = ψ(ν_p) by linearity of ψ … Cal^D_T(x′, y′) ≤ Σ_p (Σ_t x_t(p))‖ψ(ν_p) − ψ(p)‖_1 ≤ Cal^D_T(x, y) (ψ is a contraction in ℓ_1)."
results.route_rationale: ψ∘φ = id, simplex membership, linearity of ψ, ℓ1-contraction.

results.location: D.2 Lower bound for ℓ2 calibration
results.content: Equations (12)–(13) in the proof of Theorem D.2: "(12): FullSwapReg_T(x′_{1:T}, (⟨·, y_1⟩, …, ⟨·, y_T⟩)) ≤ ε·T. (13): FullSwapReg_T(x_{1:T}, (⟨·, v_1⟩, …, ⟨·, v_T⟩)) ≥ \tilde ε·T, where \tilde ε = ε^{6/7}, and the adversary has ‖v_t‖_∞ ≤ d^{−13/14} for all t, so ‖v_t‖_2 ≤ d^{1/2−13/14} = d^{−3/7}."
results.route_rationale: Exponent arithmetic (d^{1/2−13/14} = d^{−3/7}).

results.location: D.2 Lower bound for ℓ2 calibration
results.content: Theorem D.2: "There is a sufficiently small constant c > 0 so that the following holds. Write D(p, p′) = ‖p − p′‖_2 and fix any ε > 0, d ∈ ℕ. Then for any T ≤ exp(c·min{d^{1/14}, ε^{−1/7}}), there is an oblivious adversary producing a sequence y_1, …, y_T ∈ B^d_2 so that for any learning algorithm producing x_1, …, x_T ∈ Δ(B^d_2), Cal^D_T(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) ≥ ε·T."
results.route_rationale: ℓ2 lower-bound statement; internal consistency with ε̃^{7/6} = ε.

results.location: D.2 Lower bound for ℓ2 calibration
results.content: Proof of Theorem D.2 (key lines): "Write \tilde ε = ε^{6/7}. … assume d ≤ \tilde ε^{−14/6} so min{d^{1/14}, \tilde ε^{−1/6}} = min{d^{1/14}, ε^{−1/7}} = d^{1/14}. … By Lemma 4.2 with 𝒫 = B^d_2 and ‖·‖ = ‖·‖_2, for any 𝒫′ ⊂ B^d_2: FullSwapReg_T(x′_{1:T}, (⟨·, y_1⟩, …, ⟨·, y_T⟩)) ≤ ε·T. (12) … scaling 𝒳 down by 1/√d (𝒫′ = 𝒳/√d) and v_t up by d^{3/7} (v′_t = d^{3/7}·v_t): FullSwapReg_T(x′_{1:T}, (⟨·, v′_1⟩, …, ⟨·, v′_T⟩)) > \tilde ε·T·d^{−1/14} ≥ \tilde ε^{7/6}·T = ε·T … contradicting (12)."
results.route_rationale: Scaling arithmetic and the use of Lemma 4.2 (which carries a diameter factor).

results.location: E.1 Pure calibration
results.content: Theorem E.1 (Pure calibration error): "Let P ⊂ ℝ^d be a bounded convex set and ‖·‖ be an arbitrary norm with unit dual ball L := {f ∈ ℝ^d | ‖f‖_* ≤ 1}. Then, SampleTreeCal (Algorithm 3, with an appropriate choice of parameters H, L, S) guarantees that for an arbitrary sequence of outcomes y_1, …, y_T ∈ P, the ‖·‖² calibration error of its predictions x_1, …, x_T ∈ Δ(P) is bounded as follows: E[PureCal_T^{‖·‖}(p_{1:T}, y_{1:T})] ≤ ε T, for T ≥ Rate(L, ‖·‖_*) · (diam_{‖·‖}(P)/ε)^{O(Rate(P, ‖·‖)/ε²)}."
results.route_rationale: Pure-calibration bound; threshold consistency with the proof.

results.location: E.1 Pure calibration
results.content: Proof of Theorem E.1 (key lines): "By Lemma E.2 applied to M_{S(i−1)+j} = (p − y_{S(i−1)+j})·1[p_{S(i−1)+j} = p]: E‖Σ_{j=1}^S (p − y_{S(i−1)+j})·1[p_{S(i−1)+j} = p] − Σ_{j=1}^S (p − y_{S(i−1)+j})·x_i(p)‖ ≤ diam_{‖·‖}(𝒫)·√(8S·Rate(𝓛, ‖·‖_*)). … L·diam·√(8S·Rate) ≤ ε·S as long as S ≥ 8·Rate·diam²·L²/ε². (14) … Cal_T^{‖·‖}(x_{1:T/S}, \bar y_{1:T/S}) ≤ εT/S. (15) … E[PureCal_T^{‖·‖}(p_{1:T}, y_{1:T})] ≤ 2εT. The result follows by rescaling ε and our choice of L = O(Rate(𝒫, ‖·‖)/ε²)."
results.route_rationale: Concentration + combining bounds (14) and (15).

results.location: E.2 Sequential law of large numbers
results.content: Lemma E.2 ([RST15]): "Consider a convex set 𝒫 ⊂ ℝ^d, a norm ‖·‖ on ℝ^d, and let M_1, …, M_n denote a sequence of random variables adapted to a filtration (F_i)_{i ∈ [n]}. Let 𝓛 = {f | ‖f‖_* ≤ 1} be the unit ball of the dual norm ‖·‖_*. Then E[‖Σ_{i=1}^n M_i − E[M_i | F_{i−1}]‖] ≤ diam_{‖·‖}(𝒫)·√(8n·Rate(𝓛, ‖·‖_*))."
results.route_rationale: Quoted [RST15] martingale law of large numbers.

results.location: E.2 Sequential law of large numbers
results.content: Proof of Lemma E.2: "By applying an appropriate translation to 𝒫, assume 𝒫 contains the origin. Theorem 2 of [RST15] implies E[(1/n)‖Σ_i M_i − E[M_i|F_{i−1}]‖] ≤ 2·R_n(𝒫, ‖·‖) … Proposition 16 of [RST15] gives R_n(𝒫, ‖·‖) ≤ √(2ρ/n)·diam_{‖·‖}(𝒫) … In particular, R_n(𝒫, ‖·‖) ≤ diam_{‖·‖}(𝒫)·√(2·Rate(𝓛, ‖·‖_*)/n)."
results.route_rationale: Constant propagation (2·√2 = √8) from the quoted results.

findings.evidence:
Lean 4 formally refuted Lemma 2.1 as printed. With the paper's displayed Bregman definition $D_R(y\|p) := R(p) - R(y) - \langle
abla R(y), p - yangle$ (gradient at the first argument), take $R(x)=x^4$, $
abla R(x)=4x^3$, the two-point distribution $y=0,1$ each with probability $1/2$, and $p=0$. Then $\mathbb{E}[D_R(y\|0)] = 	frac{1}{2}D_R(0\|0) + 	frac{1}{2}D_R(1\|0) = 	frac{3}{2}$, while $D_R( ar y\|0) + \overline{R(y)} - R( ar y) = 	frac{3}{16} + 	frac{1}{2} - 	frac{1}{16} = 	frac{5}{8}$. Since $3/2 
e 5/8$, the printed identity is false. Under the corrected convention $D_R(y\|p) = R(y) - R(p) - \langle
abla R(p), y - pangle$ (gradient at the second argument), which every proof in the paper actually uses, the identity holds for any $R$ and any gradient (also machine-checked). So the printed Bregman definition is the typo; the lemma is true under the intended convention.

The displayed strong-convexity inequality has the wrong direction. Convexity gives $R(y) \ge R(p) + \langle\nabla R(p), y-p\rangle$, and strong convexity (in the paper's no-$1/2$ convention) adds a nonnegative quadratic term, so the correct display is $R(y) \ge R(p) + \langle\nabla R(p), y-p\rangle + \alpha\|y-p\|^2$. The printed $\le$ is an upper bound (a smoothness-type condition) and contradicts the very next sentence: $D_R(y\|p) \ge \alpha\|y-p\|^2$ expands (under the paper's operative Bregman convention) to exactly the $\ge$ form. The displayed direction and the stated equivalence cannot both be right.
findings.exact_quote: R(y) ≤ R(p) + ⟨∇R(p), y − p⟩ + α‖y − p‖²

findings.evidence:
In the proof of Lemma 2.4 (construction $R'(p)=4R(p/2)$), the bracket $2\left(\langle
abla R(p/2), yangle - \langle
abla R(p/2), pangleight)$ has the wrong sign relative to the term it replaces, and even bounding it correctly gives $12ho$, not $8ho$: $\langle
abla R(p/2), yangle \le 2ho$ and $-\langle
abla R(p/2), pangle = \langle
abla R(p/2), -pangle \le 2ho$ (central symmetry), so $2(\langle
abla R(p/2), yangle - \langle
abla R(p/2), pangle) \le 8ho$, and total $D_{R'}(y\|p) \le 4ho + 8ho = 12ho$. The asymptotic claim $O(ho)$ of Lemma 2.4 survives, but the printed bound $\le 4ho + 4ho = 8ho$ is arithmetically wrong.

The proof of the main theorem (Theorem 3.1) does not go through as printed. (1) Claim C.3 is stated as a lower bound, $\mathrm{Cal}(x) - 2\mathrm{Cal}(\tilde x) \ge (2\,\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal P)^2/H^2)T$, but the next line uses the opposite direction $\mathrm{Cal}(x) \le 2\mathrm{Cal}(\tilde x) + (2\,\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal P)^2/H^2)T$; a lower bound on $\mathrm{Cal}(x)-2\mathrm{Cal}(\tilde x)$ cannot yield an upper bound on $\mathrm{Cal}(x)$. (2) Even taking the final bound $\mathrm{Cal} \le (6\rho T)/L + (2\,\mathrm{diam}^2 T)/H^2$ at face value, the stated parameter choice $L = 12\rho/\varepsilon$, $H = \mathrm{diam}/\sqrt\varepsilon$ gives $(6\rho T)/(12\rho/\varepsilon) + (2\,\mathrm{diam}^2 T)/(\mathrm{diam}^2/\varepsilon) = \tfrac{\varepsilon T}{2} + 2\varepsilon T = 2.5\,\varepsilon T$, not $\varepsilon T$. The theorem's $O(\cdot)$-exponent statement survives constant-factor repair, but the displayed chain fails to establish $\le \varepsilon T$.
findings.exact_quote: choosing L = 12ρ/ε and H = diam(𝒫)/√ε gives that we can guarantee Cal_T^{||·||^2}(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) ≤ ε · T as long as T ≥ H^L = (diam(𝒫)/√ε)^{12ρ/ε}

findings.evidence: The displayed Bregman divergence $D_R(y\|p) := R(p) - R(y) - \langle\nabla R(y), p - y\rangle$ evaluates the gradient at the first argument $y$. The geometric description in the same paragraph ('hyperplane tangent to R at p, height difference at y') evaluates it at $p$; the proof of Lemma 2.1 expands $D_R(y\|p) = R(y) - R(p) - \langle\nabla R(p), y - p\rangle$ (gradient at $p$); and the strong-convexity equivalence $D_R(y\|p) \ge \|y-p\|^2$ only holds under the gradient-at-$p$ convention. For $R(x)=x^4$, $y=1$, $p=0$ the printed formula gives $3$ while the gradient-at-$p$ value is $1$. The definition display is the erroneous element; the paper's proofs consistently use the gradient-at-$p$ convention. The same error surfaces in paper::PROOF::0.

The body statement of Theorem 4.3 uses the exponent $\min\{d^{1/7}, \varepsilon^{-1/6}\}$, but the abstract, the introduction (Theorem 1.4), and the proof in Appendix D.1 (which derives the bound from Theorem 4.1 with exponent $(d')^{1/14}$) all use $\min\{d^{1/14}, \varepsilon^{-1/6}\}$. Since $d^{1/7} = (d^{1/14})^2$, the printed body claim is strictly stronger than what is proved, by a factor that is super-polynomial in $d$. This is a statement/proof inconsistency requiring correction.
findings.exact_quote: then for any T ≤ exp(c · min{d^{1/7}, ε^{−1/6}})

findings.evidence: The first line of the proof of Lemma 2.1 expands $D_R(y\|p)$ as $R(y) - R(p) - \langle\nabla R(p), y-p\rangle$, i.e. with the gradient at $p$ (the second argument). The paper's printed definition of $D_R$ (Section 2.3) has the gradient at $y$ (the first argument). These are different quantities for general convex $R$ (e.g. $R(x)=x^4$, $y=1$, $p=0$: $3$ vs $1$), so the proof does not follow from the stated definition. Under the implicit gradient-at-$p$ convention the derivation is algebraically sound — the inconsistency is between the proof and the definition display.

Claim C.3, equation (9), is printed as a lower bound, $\mathrm{Cal}(x) - 2\mathrm{Cal}(\tilde x) \ge (2\,\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal P)^2/H^2)T$, but its own proof derives an upper bound $\mathrm{Cal}(x) - 2\mathrm{Cal}(\tilde x) \le (2T\,\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal P)^2)/H$ — both the direction ($\ge$ vs $\le$) and the $H$-exponent ($H^2$ vs $H$) disagree. The claim as printed is moreover false: if $y_t = p_t$ for all $t$, then $\nu = p = \tilde p$ and both calibration errors vanish, giving $0 \ge (2\,\mathrm{diam}^2/H^2)T > 0$, a contradiction.

The calibration error is defined inconsistently by a factor of $T$. The introduction displays $\mathrm{Cal}_T^{\|\cdot\|} = \sum_{t=1}^T \|p_t - \nu_{p_t}\|$ (no $1/T$), while the formal definition in Section 2.1 is $\mathrm{Cal}_T^D(x_{1:T}, y_{1:T}) := \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\left(\tfrac{1}{T}\sum_t x_t(p)\right) D(\nu_p, p)$ (with $1/T$). For deterministic predictions these differ by a factor of $T$. Every theorem statement ('$\mathrm{Cal} \le \varepsilon T$') and every proof (e.g. Corollary C.5) uses the un-normalised sum, so the spurious $1/T$ in the formal definition is the likely typo, but the two displayed definitions are mutually inconsistent as printed.

In the proof of Theorem 4.3 the paper asserts $\mathrm{diam}_{\|\cdot\|_\infty}(\mathcal P') = 1$ for $\mathcal P' = [-1,1]^{d'}$. The diameter (pairwise) of the cube $[-1,1]^{d'}$ in the $\infty$-norm is $2$: $\|(1,\dots,1) - (-1,\dots,-1)\|_\infty = 2$. The value $1$ is the radius, not the diameter. Consequently Lemma 4.2 yields $\mathrm{FullSwapReg} \le 2\varepsilon T$, not $\varepsilon T$, and the printed contradiction with the lower bound $\ge \varepsilon T$ does not go through; it is repairable by absorbing the constant into the 'sufficiently small' $c$ (or scaling $\varepsilon$), but as printed the diameter evaluation is wrong.

In the proof of Theorem D.2, equation (12) claims $\mathrm{FullSwapReg}_T \le \varepsilon T$ 'by Lemma 4.2 with $\mathcal P = \mathcal B^d_2$ and $\|\cdot\| = \|\cdot\|_2$, for any $\mathcal P' \subset \mathcal B^d_2$', but the quoted Lemma 4.2 gives $\mathrm{FullSwapReg} \le \varepsilon \cdot T \cdot \mathrm{diam}_{\|\cdot\|_*}(\mathcal P')$ with $\|\cdot\|_* = \|\cdot\|_2$. For the set actually used, $\mathcal P' = \mathcal X/\sqrt d$ with $\mathcal X \subset [-1,1]^d$, $\mathrm{diam}_{\|\cdot\|_2}(\mathcal P') \le 2$ (attained, e.g. $\mathcal X = \{-1,1\}^d$), so Lemma 4.2 only gives $\mathrm{FullSwapReg} \le 2\varepsilon T$. The scaled lower bound $> \tilde\varepsilon^{7/6}T = \varepsilon T$ then does not contradict $2\varepsilon T$; the argument closes only after a constant adjustment. Same diameter/radius mishandling as in paper::PROOF::9.

The printed proof of Lemma C.4 bounds only the single term $\|\tilde p_h - p_h\|^2 \le (\pi^2/6)\,\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal P)^2$ and then stops, but the lemma's conclusion is the sum $\sum_{h=1}^H \|p_h - \tilde p_h\|^2 \le 2\,\mathrm{diam}(\mathcal P)^2$. A per-term bound does not imply the sum bound (summed over $H$ terms it gives $H\cdot(\pi^2/6)\,\mathrm{diam}^2$, which exceeds $2\,\mathrm{diam}^2$ for $H \ge 2$). The lemma is true (machine-checked, see paper::LEMMA::6) via $\tilde p_h - p_h = (y_h - p_h)/h$ and $\sum_{h\ge 2} 1/h^2 \le 1$, but that summation argument is absent from the printed proof.
findings.exact_quote: which implies that ‖\tilde p_h − p_h‖² ≤ (π²/6) · diam(𝒫)² < 2 diam(𝒫)². □

summary:
Verified the mathematics of 'High-Dimensional Calibration from Swap Regret' (Fishelson, Golowich, Mohri, Schneider; NeurIPS 2025; arXiv 2505.21460). 43 self-contained objects were extracted (11 theorems, 9 lemmas, 10 equations, 13 proofs) and routed: 40 to informal review (verify-math) and 3 to formal Lean 4 verification (verify-math-lean) against the shared pre-existing project MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper (kept, not deleted — it predates this session).

Formal results: Lemma 2.1 as printed was REFUTED in Lean — under the paper's displayed Bregman definition (gradient at the first argument) the proper-scoring-rule identity is false; a concrete counterexample (R(x)=x^4, two-point distribution, p=0) gives LHS 3/2 vs RHS 5/8. Under the gradient-at-p convention that every proof in the paper actually uses, the identity holds (also machine-checked). Lemma C.4 (cumulative-averages inequality) and the φ/ψ construction of Lemma D.1 both PASSED machine-checked proofs.

The main mathematical claims are not invalidated, but the manuscript contains a cluster of genuine errors that would need a correction: (1) the printed Bregman divergence definition is inconsistent with its own geometric description, the proof of Lemma 2.1, and all subsequent usage — a definitional typo that also breaks Lemma 2.1 as printed; (2) the displayed strong-convexity inequality has the wrong direction (≤ should be ≥); (3) the proof of Theorem 3.1 (the main upper bound) does not go through as printed — Claim C.3 is stated with the wrong sign/direction (its own proof establishes an upper bound, not the lower bound claimed) and the parameter choice L=12ρ/ε, H=diam/√ε yields 2.5εT, not εT (the O(·)-exponent statement survives constant repair); (4) Lemma 2.4's proof has a sign error in a bracket and the bound should be 12ρ, not 8ρ; (5) the proof of Lemma C.4 bounds only one term instead of the sum (the lemma itself is true, as Lean confirmed); (6) the body of Theorem 4.3 states min{d^{1/7}, ε^{−1/6}} where the abstract, introduction and proof use d^{1/14}; (7) the lower-bound proofs of Theorems 4.3 and D.2 mishandle diameter vs radius (diam_{‖·‖_∞}([−1,1]^{d'}) is 2, not 1, and the diameter factor from Lemma 4.2 is dropped in eq. (12)), both repairable by constant absorption; (8) the calibration-error definition carries an inconsistent 1/T factor between the introduction and Section 2.1.

Every finding is at confidence ≥ 0.7 (range 0.8–0.95); the strongest is the machine-checked refutation of Lemma 2.1 as printed. All findings are classified 'minor' because the paper's central claims (the calibration upper and lower bounds) are big-O statements that survive the constant-factor, direction, and definitional fixes, and the two Lean-passed lemmas corroborate the surrounding machinery. No Lean result was FAILED, so no informal fallbacks were needed; the Lean project was kept on disk (pre-existing shared project). Verdict: MINOR_ERRORS at confidence 0.8.
